title: Pushes and pulls
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Physics: in the playground, how toys work, pushes and pulls around us, changing movement. No textbook needed.
summary: Everything that moves was pushed or pulled. Your child finds pushes and pulls in the park, in toys and at home. They find that things never start moving by themselves, that a moving thing keeps going until something stops it, and that every push gets a push back. They meet gravity, the pull of the Earth, and friction, the rubbing force that slows things down. They also draw their first force arrows.
builds_on: This is the first rung. Class 2 adds squashing, stretching, speed and falling. Class 3 measures forces in newtons and studies friction. Class 4 explores balance, simple machines, pressure and floating. Class 5 puts many forces together in force diagrams, with air and water resistance and rockets. Separate rungs on gravity (Class 5) and magnets (Classes 3 and 5) branch off this one.
subconcepts: a force is a push or a pull
pushes and pulls in the playground: swing, slide, see-saw
how toys work: pushes, pulls and wound-up springs
things never start moving by themselves
a moving thing keeps going until something stops it
a bigger push makes things go faster and further
heavy things are harder to start and to stop
forces speed things up, slow them down, stop them and turn them
every push gets a push back
the Earth pulls everything down (gravity, first meeting)
rubbing slows things down (friction, first meeting)
air and water can push too
a force can be drawn as an arrow
goals: By the end your child can show a push and a pull with their body and with objects, and name a force as a push or a pull.
By the end your child can explain that things do not start, stop or turn by themselves: a push or pull has to do it.
By the end your child can show that a bigger push makes a car go further, and that a heavy basket needs a bigger push than a light one.
By the end your child can feel and describe the push back from a wall or the floor, and say that the Earth pulls everything down.
By the end your child can draw a force as an arrow pointing the way it pushes or pulls.
By the end your child can predict before testing, and say whether the guess was right.
words: to press something away from you
the way something is going: left, right, up, down
the push you feel from whatever you push
the pull of the Earth that makes things fall down
the rubbing force that slows things down
a line with a point that shows which way a force goes
to guess what will happen before you try it

days.title: Push or pull?
days.goal: Notice that we move things by pushing and pulling them, and meet the word force.

steps.title: Move the chair
steps.do: Put a light plastic chair in the middle of the room. Ask your child: 'Can you make the chair come to you without walking to it?' Let them try. They may tie a dupatta to it and pull. Then ask: 'Now make it go far away from you.' Say: 'When you made it come to you, that was a pull. When you made it go away, that was a push.'

steps.title: Simon says push, Simon says pull
steps.do: Play Simon Says with actions: 'Simon says push a door', 'Simon says pull a drawer', 'Simon says pull up your socks', 'Simon says press a button'. Sometimes leave out 'Simon says' ('kick a ball'), and your child must freeze. After each action ask: 'Push or pull?' Kicking and pressing a button are pushes. Opening the fridge is a pull. If they are unsure, ask: 'Did it go away from you or come towards you?'

steps.title: Push and pull hunt
steps.do: Walk round the home with a sheet folded into two columns, PUSH and PULL. At each thing, your child does the action and draws a tiny picture in the right column: a drawer (pull), a switch (push), a zip (pull), kneading atta (push), rolling a chapati with a rolling pin (push), pressing a murukku press (push), ringing a cycle bell (push), drawing a curtain (pull). Some jobs need both, like sweeping with a broom or opening and shutting a door. Ask: 'Which jobs needed a push AND a pull?'

steps.title: The word force, and the push-pull dance
steps.do: Say: 'Scientists have one word for every push and every pull. They call it a force.' Let your child say 'force' three times in a funny voice. Then dance it. Put on any song and stand palm to palm with your child. When the music is loud, one of you pushes gently and the other leans into the push. When it is soft, hold hands and lean apart, pulling. After the song ask: 'When I pushed you, could you feel me? When you pushed me, did your hands feel anything?' (Yes. When you push someone, you feel a push back on your hands.)

need: a sheet of paper and a pencil

days.title: Playground forces
days.goal: Find pushes and pulls on swings, slides, see-saws and balls, and draw a force as an arrow.

steps.title: Park scientists
steps.do: Go to a park or playground if there is one nearby. If not, look at a picture of one together and ask the same questions. At the swing ask: 'How does the swing start moving? What makes it go higher?' (Someone pushes it. A push at the right moment makes it go higher.) At the slide: 'Who pushes you down the slide?' (Nobody. The Earth pulls you down. That pull is called gravity.) At the see-saw: 'How do you make your side go up?' (Push the ground with your feet.) Ask: 'Why does the heavier person's side go down?' (The Earth pulls the heavier person down harder.) Then play catch: 'Did I push or pull the ball to throw it?' (Push.) Look up at a bird. Ask: 'What stops the bird from falling down?' (Their wings push air down, and the air pushes the bird up.)

steps.title: Tug of war and palm push
steps.do: Do Activity a1: tug of war with a dupatta, then palm-to-palm pushing. Ask: 'Why did the dupatta move towards the winner?' (Their pull was bigger.) 'When nobody moves, are we still pushing?' (Yes. Both pushes are equal, so nothing moves.)

steps.title: Draw an arrow, and Ibn Sina's question
steps.do: At home, your child draws one thing from the park. Show them how to add an arrow. The arrow starts on the thing and points the way the push or pull goes. A big push gets a long arrow, a small push a short one. Then ask: 'When you throw a ball, your hand lets go. So what keeps the ball flying?' Listen to their idea first. Then tell them about Ibn Sina, a great doctor and thinker in Persia about 1,000 years ago (voice v2): what he thought, and what we think now.

days.title: How toys work
days.goal: Discover that every moving toy needs a push or a pull, sometimes stored in a spring.

steps.title: Toy parade
steps.do: Your child brings five toys that can move: a car, a ball, a lattu (top), a pull-along toy, a yo-yo, a wind-up or pull-back car if you have one. Ask about each: 'How do we make it move?'

steps.title: Sort the toys, and the hidden spring
steps.do: Make two places on the floor with paper labels PUSH and PULL. Your child plays with each toy and puts it on the right label. A pushed car goes on push. A pull-along toy goes on pull. A lattu goes on pull, because you pull the string to spin it. A yo-yo needs both, so put it in the middle. Then show a pull-back car or a wind-up toy. Pull it backwards on the floor and let go. It zooms off. Ask: 'Did it start by itself?' (No. Pulling it back wound up a spring inside. The spring holds your pull and gives it back as a push when you let go.)

steps.title: Push-Pull Path
steps.do: Print the game g1. Play it with coins as counters and a die. On each square, your child does the action and says 'push' or 'pull' before the next turn.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do the first two sections of Worksheet ws1 together. Read each question aloud. Your child answers by pointing, sorting or saying, and you write their words for them. Keep the rest for Day 4.

need: a pull-back or wind-up toy if you have one
the printed game, a die and two coins

days.title: Every push gets a push back
days.goal: Feel that a wall, a floor and a friend all push back, and hear the story.

steps.title: Story: Kavya and the Wall That Pushed Back
steps.do: Read the story aloud slowly. Don't explain it. Ask two of the story questions: 'Why did Kavya roll backwards when she pushed Chintu's box?' and 'When you walk, what pushes you forward?' Accept any answers today.

steps.title: Push the wall, the cushion and the water
steps.do: Your child puts both palms on a wall and pushes hard. Ask: 'Look at your hands. Why are they squashed and pink?' (The wall is pushing back.) Now push a cushion. Then put a hand flat on the water in a bucket and push down. Ask: 'Which pushed back the hardest? Which let your hand go in?' (The wall pushed back hardest. The water let the hand in.) Say: 'Everything is made of tiny bits too small to see, called atoms. When you press on something, its atoms push back on the atoms of your hand. In a wall they are packed tight, so they push back hard. In water they slide aside.' Then your child stands in socks on a smooth floor and pushes the wall. They slide backwards. Throw a ball for them to catch and say: 'The ball pushed your hands, and your hands pushed the ball to stop it.'

steps.title: Mountain pose: feel the floor push
steps.do: Stand together in mountain pose (tadasana): feet together, arms by your sides, standing tall and still. Ask your child to close their eyes and feel their feet pressing into the floor. Ask: 'Which way are you pushing the floor?' (Down.) 'Which way is the floor pushing you?' (Up. That's why we don't sink into it.) Then walk across the room very slowly, feeling each foot press down and back. Ask: 'Which way does the floor push you now?' (Forwards.) 'What if the floor were as slippery as ice?' (We couldn't walk.) Say: 'You can't push anything without being pushed back. This is true everywhere in the universe.'

steps.title: Finish the core worksheet
steps.do: Do section C of Worksheet ws1: the arrow puzzles and the two 'why' questions. For the arrow puzzles, your child points the way the force goes and you tick it. Say their 'why' answers aloud together, and write them down for your child.

days.title: Big push, small push, heavy and light
days.goal: Find out that a bigger push makes things go further, and heavy things need bigger pushes.

steps.title: Gentle or strong?
steps.do: Roll a ball to your child very gently, then a bit harder. Ask: 'Which came faster? What did I do differently?' (A bigger push.)

steps.title: Ramp race
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child guesses first, then tests. Put a sticky note where the car stops each time, and measure with heel-to-toe steps. Ask: 'Was your guess right? Is it OK if a guess is wrong?' Say: 'Scientists make wrong guesses all the time. Testing is how they find out.'

steps.title: Heavy and light basket
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Push an empty laundry basket or cardboard box across the floor with one finger. Then fill it with books and try the same one-finger push. Then slide it gently towards your child and let them stop it, first empty, then full. Ask: 'Which was harder to start? Which was harder to stop?' (The full one, both times.) Say: 'Heavy things are harder to start and harder to stop. That is why a loaded bus needs strong brakes.'

steps.title: Who needs the biggest push?
steps.do: Say pairs, and your child chooses which needs the bigger push to start moving: a cycle or a lorry? An empty school bag or a full one? An empty pram or a pram with a baby in it? (The heavier one each time.) Ask: 'Why does a lorry full of bricks take so long to stop?' (It is heavy, so it is hard to stop.)

need: a flat board or big book for a ramp
a laundry basket or cardboard box

days.title: Lazy things, falling things and rubbing things
days.goal: See that things keep doing what they are doing until a force changes it, meet the Earth's pull, and meet friction.

steps.title: The coin that stays
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Put a playing card on top of a steel tumbler and a coin on the card. Flick the card away fast, and the coin drops into the tumbler. Ask: 'Why didn't the coin fly away with the card?' (Nobody pushed the coin sideways, so it stayed where it was. Then the Earth pulled it straight down.) Then put a small toy in a toy truck, roll the truck into a book, and watch the toy fly forward. Ask: 'Why do we wear seat belts?' (When the car stops, we keep going unless something holds us.)

steps.title: Which floor slows it most?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Roll the same car down the same ramp onto tiles, a mat and a towel. Mark where it stops each time. Ask: 'Nobody touched the car. Why did it stop on the towel?' Accept 'the towel held it back'. Say: 'The rough towel rubs on the wheels and slows them. Scientists call this rubbing force friction.'

steps.title: What pulls things down?
steps.do: Hold a ball, a spoon and a crumpled paper above a cushion and let go one at a time. Ask: 'Which way did they all go?' (Down.) 'Has anything ever fallen up?' Say: 'The whole Earth pulls everything towards it. That pull is called gravity.' Then blow a paper ball across the table with a straw and ask: 'Did I touch it?' (No, the air pushed it.) 'What pushes a boat's sail?' (The wind.)

steps.title: Ball goal
steps.do: Make a goal with two slippers. Roll the ball slowly across the room. Your child taps it once from the side to turn it into the goal. Then they speed it up with a tap from behind, and slow it down with a hand in front. After each, ask: 'Did your push speed it up, slow it down, stop it or turn it?'

need: a toy truck and a small toy
a towel and a mat or rug
a ball, a spoon, paper, a straw

days.title: Teach it back
days.goal: Show what you know about pushes and pulls, weigh an old idea, and talk about big questions.

steps.title: Make it move
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. Read each question aloud. Your child answers by pointing, drawing or saying. For the arrow items, they show the direction with their finger first. On another day, try the puzzles on Worksheet ws3 together.

steps.title: Aristotle or Galileo?
steps.do: Talk about voice v1. Say: 'Aristotle, a famous thinker in Greece more than 2,000 years ago, said moving things stop because stopping is natural. Much later, in Italy, Galileo said things only stop because something slows them down.' Ask: 'Our car went further on the tiles than on the towel. Which of them does that agree with?' (Galileo.) Then ask: 'Can a ball start rolling all by itself?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher and you are a student who knows nothing. Ask the check questions in a confused voice ('How do I open the fridge? Do I push it?') and let them explain and show. Ask them to show the push back with a wall, and to tell you what pulls a mango down. Then act out a short play: one of you is a door, the other pushes it, and the door pushes back just as hard. Last, ask them to show you one push and one pull that you did not find this week, and to show the family the push-pull toy from the project.

need: the push-pull toy from the project

Imran, a boy, pulls a box on wheels towards him, to the left. Show his pull.

A ball rolls on a floor that is perfectly smooth and goes on for ever. There is no air. What happens to the ball?
opts: it stops by itself after a while

sections.p: A lorry and a cycle roll towards you at the same speed. Which needs the bigger push to stop?

experiments.title: Ramp race
experiments.question: Does a higher ramp make the car go further?
need: a flat board or big hardback book
books to build the ramp up
steps: Lean the board on one book to make a low ramp.
Let the car go from the top. Do not push it, just let go.
Put a sticky note where the car stops.
Add a second book to make the ramp higher. Let the car go from the same place and mark it.
Add a third book and try again.
Compare the three marks and count the steps to each.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'Which ramp will make the car go furthest: low, middle or high?' Write the guess down.
experiments.observe: Where the car stops each time, measured in heel-to-toe steps.
experiments.why: On a higher ramp, the Earth's pull has longer to speed the car up as it comes down, so the car reaches the floor going faster and rolls further before rubbing on the floor slows it down. A bigger push (or a longer pull from gravity) makes a bigger change in movement.
experiments.safety: Keep the floor clear so nobody trips over the ramp.

experiments.title: Which floor slows it most?
experiments.question: Which floor makes a rolling car stop soonest?
need: the ramp from e1 (two books high)
steps: Put the end of the ramp on the tiles. Let the car go and mark where it stops.
Lay the towel at the end of the ramp. Let the car go from the same place and mark it.
Do the same with the mat or rug.
Compare the three marks.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which floor will stop the car quickest?'
experiments.observe: How far the car rolls on each floor.
experiments.why: Rough surfaces rub against the wheels more. This rubbing force, friction, slows the car down sooner. On smooth tiles there is less rubbing, so the car rolls further. If there were no rubbing and no air at all, it would never stop.
experiments.safety: Keep the floor clear so nobody trips over the ramp.

experiments.title: Heavy and light basket
experiments.question: Is a heavy thing harder to start and to stop than a light one?
need: a plastic laundry basket or a strong cardboard box
steps: Push the empty basket with one finger. Does it move easily?
Fill it with books. Push it with one finger again.
Gently slide the empty basket towards your child, who stops it with both hands.
Now slide the full basket gently towards them. Which was harder to stop?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the full basket be easier, harder or the same to start? To stop?'
experiments.observe: How hard your child has to push to start each basket and to stop it.
experiments.why: The heavier something is, the harder it is to change how it moves. A full basket needs a bigger push to get going and a bigger push to stop. Scientists call this inertia. Your child will meet the word later.
experiments.safety: Slide the full basket slowly. It should never hit toes.

experiments.title: The coin that stays
experiments.question: If you pull something out from under a coin very fast, does the coin go with it?
need: a toy truck and a small toy passenger
steps: Put the card on top of the tumbler and the coin in the middle of the card.
Flick the card sideways, hard and fast, with your finger.
Watch where the coin goes.
Now put the small toy in the back of the toy truck and roll the truck into the book.
Watch where the toy goes when the truck stops.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the coin fly away with the card or drop into the tumbler? Will the toy stop with the truck?'
experiments.observe: The coin drops into the tumbler. The toy keeps going and flies out when the truck stops.
experiments.why: Things keep doing what they were doing until a force changes it. The card was flicked away so fast that it hardly pushed the coin, so the coin stayed where it was and then gravity pulled it down into the tumbler. The toy was moving with the truck. When the book stopped the truck, nothing stopped the toy, so it kept going. A seat belt is the push that stops you.
experiments.safety: Flick the card away from faces.

activities.title: Tug of war and palm push
steps: Hold opposite ends of the dupatta and pull gently.
Let your child win once by pulling harder.
Then push palm to palm with the same strength so nobody moves.
Ask what happened in each case.
activities.outcome: Your child feels that a bigger pull wins, and that equal pushes cancel out so nothing moves.

project.title: Make a push-pull toy
steps: Choose a toy to make: a small box pulled along on a string, or a paper ball you blow across the floor with a straw.
Make it from things at home: a matchbox or small box, string, a straw, paper and tape.
Test it: how do you make it go? Push or pull?
Make it go further. What did you change?
Show it to the family on Day 7, draw an arrow for its push or pull, and explain it.
project.outcome: A home-made toy, an arrow drawing, and a short show-and-tell.

game.title: Push-Pull Path
rules: Do the action on your square and say 'push' or 'pull'. Get it right: stay. Wrong: go back 1.
Squares with a star let you roll again.
squares: Slide down: who pulls you? Back 1
Car on a towel: slow down, miss a turn
Push a wall: feel it push back
Full basket: hard to start, back 1

big: Why does a mango fall down from the tree and not up?
Could anything ever start moving all by itself?
Does your bed push you up even when you are asleep?
When a magnet attracts a pin, is it pushing or pulling?

challenge.q: People used to think things stop moving because stopping is natural. Is that true? What made our car stop?
challenge.hint: Try the car on tiles and on a towel. If stopping were natural, would the floor matter? Galileo noticed that the smoother the surface, the further a ball rolls, and guessed that with nothing at all to slow it, it would roll for ever.

challenge.q: We say 'the wind pushed the door shut'. Can air push? How could you show it without touching the door?
challenge.hint: Blow through a straw at a paper ball, or wave a newspaper at a feather. Air is real, though you can't see it. It is made of tiny particles, and moving air pushes on whatever it hits.

challenge.q: People say 'a big strong person can push anything without getting pushed'. Is that true?
challenge.hint: Push a wall as hard as you can and look at your hands. Even the strongest wrestler gets pushed back exactly as hard as they push. Big people just don't slide as easily, because they are heavier and their feet grip the floor.

perspectives.view: Pulling a cart is easier on a smooth road than in a muddy field. Ask: why would mud make the bullocks work harder? What do the bullocks push against with their hooves?
In kabaddi, one raider runs into the other team's half, and the whole team holds them back together. Ask: who wins, one person pulling or many pulling together? Why?

An ant needs to carry food home, and a crumb can be much bigger than the ant. An ant can carry many times their own weight, by pushing against the ground with six legs. Ants also carry big crumbs together. Ask: if you were as strong as an ant for your size, what could you lift?

A fish pushes water backwards with their tail, and the water pushes the fish forwards. A bird pushes air down with their wings, and the air pushes the bird up. Ask: what do you push against when you walk?

Bharatanatyam dancers stamp the floor to make the bells on their ankles ring. Each time a foot hits the floor, the floor pushes back. Ask: could you jump or dance at all if the floor didn't push back?

voices.who: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), Greece, and Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italy
voices.idea: Aristotle taught that the natural state of things is to be still, so a moving thing stops on its own unless something keeps pushing it.
voices.then: For almost 2,000 years most people agreed. Galileo rolled balls down ramps and onto smooth surfaces and saw that the smoother the surface, the further the ball rolled. He argued that a ball on a perfectly smooth, flat surface would keep rolling for ever.
voices.now: Galileo was right, and Isaac Newton later made it the first law of motion. Things only slow down because something, like rubbing or air, pushes back on them.
voices.ask: Our car went further on the tiles than on the towel. Which idea does that agree with, Aristotle's or Galileo's? What test would change your mind?

voices.who: Ibn Sina (980–1037), a doctor and thinker in Persia
voices.idea: Ibn Sina disagreed with Aristotle's idea that the air keeps pushing a thrown stone along. He said the thrower gives the stone an inner 'inclination' (mayl) to keep moving, which is used up as the air and the ground resist it.
voices.then: Later thinkers in Europe, like Jean Buridan in the 1300s, developed a similar idea they called 'impetus'. It was a big step away from Aristotle.
voices.now: Today we say a moving thing keeps moving unless a force, like friction or the push of air, slows it down. Ibn Sina was right that the air does not keep it going, and right that resistance slows it. Newton later made this a clear law, with no 'inclination' inside the thing.
voices.ask: Is a thrown ball carrying something inside it that runs out, or does it just keep going until something slows it? How could you test it?

books.title: Forces Make Things Move
books.author: Kimberly Brubaker Bradley
books.why: A clear picture book about pushes, pulls and why things move.

books.title: Rosie Revere, Engineer
books.author: Andrea Beaty
books.why: A girl builds machines that fail, and learns that failing is how you get better. Good with the project.

books.author: Ashley Spires
books.why: Making something, getting frustrated, and trying again.

check.q: Show me a push and a pull. What is another name for a push or a pull?
check.a: Any correct action. A push or a pull is called a force.

check.q: Can a ball start rolling all by itself?
check.a: No, something has to push or pull it.

check.q: How do you make the car go further?
check.a: Give it a bigger push, or use a higher ramp.

check.q: Which is harder to start and stop: a full basket or an empty one?
check.a: The full one, because it is heavier.

check.q: What happens when you push a wall?
check.a: The wall pushes back on your hands.

check.q: What pulls a mango down from the tree?
Why did the car stop sooner on the towel?
check.a: The rough towel rubbed on the wheels and slowed it down (friction).

story.title: Kavya and the Wall That Pushed Back
text: The rain had been falling on Kavya's old building in Hyderabad for three whole days, and Kavya was cross. She was cross with the rain for keeping her indoors. She was cross with the grey sky. But most of all she was cross with her baby brother, Chintu, who had been born in the summer and had been the centre of everything ever since.
"Everyone looks at Chintu," she said to nobody. "Chintu sneezed. Chintu smiled. Chintu did a burp." She stamped to the door of their room. "I don't need anyone. I'm going to push everything away."

She put both hands flat on the wooden door and pushed it shut. Bang. That felt good. But something strange happened as she pushed: she felt the door pushing her hands back. She took her hands away and looked at them. Pink, a bit squashed. She pushed the door again, gently this time, and there it was: the door was pressing back on her palms, exactly as hard as she pressed it.

She went to the wall, the thick old wall that had stood since before her Ammamma was born, and she pushed it as hard as she could. She pushed until her face went red and her elbows shook. The wall did not move at all. But her hands hurt, and her feet slid backwards on the floor.
"Ammamma," she called, "the wall is pushing me!"

Ammamma, her grandmother, was sitting on the mat, folding clothes, with Chintu asleep beside her like a small warm loaf. She did not laugh. She put down the shirt she was folding. "Of course it is," she said. "Nothing in the whole world can be pushed without pushing back. Not doors. Not walls. Not even the floor under your feet. When you walk, you push the floor behind you, and the floor pushes you forward. That is the only reason you can walk at all."

Kavya thought about this. She walked across the room very slowly, feeling each foot press down and back, and the floor quietly pressing her up and on. She had walked ten thousand times and never once said thank you to the floor.

The next day the rain stopped. The courtyard was shining, and the older children brought out their roller skates. Kavya's cousin Imran lent her his old pair, and Chintu, who could now sit up, was placed in a cardboard box on wheels that Imran had made, and everyone took turns pulling him around.

When it was Kavya's turn, she was still a little bit cross. She stood behind Chintu's box on her skates and gave it a big push to send it away from her. Whoosh, off went the box across the wet stone. But Kavya went whooshing too, backwards, the other way, her arms flapping, until she bumped into the water tank and sat down with a splash.

Everyone laughed, and so, after a moment, did Kavya. But as she sat there in the puddle, she understood something she could not quite put into words. When she pushed Chintu away, she had been pushed away too. You could not do one without the other.

She got up. She skated carefully to the box, where Chintu was waving his fat hands at her. She held out her hands, and he grabbed her fingers with his tight baby grip. And then Kavya pulled. Gently. And as she pulled him towards her, she rolled towards him, and they met in the middle of the courtyard, the box and the girl, and spun round once, slowly, together.
Ammamma was watching from the balcony. She did not say anything. She just smiled and went back inside to fold the clothes.
story.epiphany: Newton's third law, felt in the body at age 6: every push or pull comes in a pair. You can't push without being pushed back, and when you pull something towards you, you move towards it too. The story turns when Kavya slides backwards as she pushes Chintu's box away.
ask: When Kavya pushed the door, what did she feel? Try it now with a door.
Why did Kavya roll backwards when she pushed Chintu's box?
When you walk, what pushes you forward?
What happened when she pulled instead of pushed?
Can you think of anything you can push that doesn't push you back?

ideas.idea: You can't push anything without being pushed back.
ideas.more: Push a wall and feel your hands squash. Stand in socks on a smooth floor and push a friend: you both move apart. Scientists call this Newton's third law. You can feel it long before you can name it.

ideas.idea: Nothing starts, stops or turns by itself.
ideas.more: A ball on the floor stays there for ever until something pushes it. A rolling ball would roll for ever if nothing slowed it down. That was Galileo's great idea, and the coin on the card and the toy in the truck show it.

ideas.idea: We walk, swim and fly by pushing the world.
ideas.more: Feet push the floor back. Fish push water back. Birds push air down. Everything that moves itself does it by pushing on something else: the ground, the water or the air.

unknowns: Why does a moving thing keep moving if nothing stops it? Scientists can describe it perfectly, but why the universe works this way, nobody knows.
What is the pull that brings a mango down from the tree? We call it gravity, and we can measure it very precisely, but what gravity really is is still one of the biggest mysteries in science.

Why does a rough towel slow a car more than smooth tiles? The simple answer is bumps catching on bumps. But scientists who study rubbing at the scale of atoms say the full story is still not worked out.
